title: A king on a donkey (Luke 19:28–40)
hook: crowds wave branches and throw coats on the road for a man on a borrowed donkey

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus, called out of the tomb, and your line: jesus wept. What grief did you let yourself feel? Today, the last week begins, and the road goes up into Jerusalem. Day sixty-one.

Motorcades. Tinted windows. Security in dark suits. A red carpet. That's how power tends to arrive. This arrival starts on the road over the Mount of Olives toward Jerusalem, with the city filling up for Passover. Jesus sends two disciples ahead to a village with strange instructions: you'll find a colt tied up that no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it. If anyone asks why, say this: "The Lord hath need of him." They go, and it's exactly as he said. The owners ask, the disciples answer, and the owners let it go. A borrowed donkey. Today's word: hosanna.
screen: `MOTORCADES AND RED CARPETS.` → `A COLT NO ONE HAS RIDDEN.` → `THE LORD HATH NEED OF HIM.`

segments.voice: They throw their coats over the colt, and set Jesus on it. And as he rides, people spread their coats on the road in front of him, a red carpet made of whatever they're wearing. As he comes down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of his followers starts shouting, in Luke's words in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest." Now today's word. Luke doesn't use it, but Matthew, Mark and John do, and it's the word the crowd shouted, in Matthew: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, hoshia na, and it means save, please. It comes from Psalm 118, the psalm the crowd is quoting, where the King James Bible renders it: "Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD." Over time it became a shout of praise, but underneath it's a cry for help: save us, now. And John adds the palm branches, which is why churches call this Palm Sunday. Why a donkey? The prophet Zechariah had said Jerusalem's king would come "lowly, and riding upon an ass." And in the next verse the horse is cut off from Jerusalem, and the king speaks peace. This is a king arriving in a way no emperor would. Some of the Pharisees in the crowd tell him to quiet his followers. And he says: "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out." Christians still shout hosanna in worship. Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, Lutherans and others sing it in the communion prayers, before the bread and cup are shared.
screen: `COATS ON THE ROAD.` · `HOSANNA: SAVE, PLEASE.` · `A DONKEY, NOT A WAR HORSE.` · `THE STONES WOULD CRY OUT.` · then, large: `BLESSED BE THE KING THAT COMETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. The crowd laid down their coats, the thing they had on them, so someone else's way would be smoother. Think of one person in your life whose road could use smoothing today. What could you lay down for them? Your turn to talk. Your preferred plan. Your seat. An hour of your time. Your need to be right. Picture yourself laying it down in front of them. If you pray, you can say the old word, hosanna: save, please. The bell holds the time.
Hosanna. From the Hebrew hoshia na: save, please. A cry for help that became a shout of praise, sung for a king on a donkey.
Your line: the stones would cry out. Today, lay something down for someone, quietly, the way they laid down their coats. Day sixty-one.

howItsDone: Many churches keep Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week, with palm branches, a procession and readings of the entry into Jerusalem. In many churches the Sanctus, sung in the communion prayers, ends with Hosanna in the highest.

original.note: Hebrew, from Psalm 118: save, please. The Greek Gospels carried it over as hosanna.

trapdoor: what you thought: hosanna is just a church word for hooray.
what it means: save, please: a cry for help from a psalm, shouted for a king who arrives on a borrowed donkey.
what a scholar hears: hoshia na comes from Psalm 118:25, and the donkey fulfills Zechariah 9:9, a king lowly and riding upon an ass.

notes: Luke's account has no 'hosanna' and no palms; the script says so and draws hosanna from Matthew 21:9 and palms from John 12:13.
Hosanna from Hebrew hoshi'ah na (Psalm 118:25); Psalm 118 as one of the Hallel psalms sung by pilgrims. Confirm.
Donkey as a sign of peace versus horse of war: a common reading of Zechariah 9:9–10; confirm the simplification.
Sanctus/Benedictus with 'Hosanna in the highest' in Catholic, Orthodox (Anaphora), Anglican and Lutheran liturgies; confirm the church list.
The Pharisees' request (Luke 19:39) is stated neutrally as 'some of the Pharisees in the crowd'.
